name: Followers of Set: Doctrine, Cults and Temples (Clanbook)

pages.name: Theophidian Doctrine: The Aeons and the Path of Sutekh

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

The Followers of Set are as much a cult as a clan, and their theology (called Theophidian doctrine) is more structured than most Kindred realize. It holds that the world is a bubble of light and life within an endless black sea called Nun, the Primeval Ocean. The creator, Atum-Ra, arose from Nun and raised the mound of earth that became the world. Setite doctrine calls Atum-Ra a small and wicked Demiurge rather than a true universal god. The Demiurge birthed lesser gods called the Aeons to help shape and rule the world; the Aeons, in turn, created and over-refined humanity.

In the First Age the Aeons lived among humanity directly. Set's transformation into the first vampire is said to have forced the Aeons to withdraw from the material world. Now they rule only spiritually, weaving religions, governments, commerce and war into a web (the Setites call it Maat, the Order of Things) meant to ensnare human souls. Every mask an Aeon wears — Ra, Osiris, Jehovah, Zeus, Marduk — is simply one more name for the same jailer. Setites deliberately identify Set with foreign gods (Bacchus, Mars, Pluto, Typhon, Shiva, Damballah, and so on) to spread his worship, but never with Ra, Osiris or Horus, who are held to be masks of the Demiurge's own agents.

The Path of Sutekh: Because Setite cults eventually diverged on interpretation, the original Theophidian teaching split into two related Paths of Enlightenment: the well-known Path of Typhon, which teaches revelry in universal corruption, and the Path of Sutekh, which teaches followers to push past desire and degradation entirely in search of gnosis. Some cults teach Typhon first and reveal Sutekh only to advanced initiates; others simply use the corruption of the Path of Typhon to make the doctrine palatable before revealing that degradation was the entire point all along. A character following the Path of Sutekh may switch to the Path of Typhon (or vice versa) at no cost beyond her Path rating dropping to 3; a Theophidian at 3 or less may flip-flop freely, but doing so prevents ever advancing in either Path.

Ethics of the Path of Sutekh:

  • Gather information — secret and otherwise — and learn how it applies to the resurrection of Set, the true nature of divinity, and the origin and fate of the world.
  • Subjugate the Beast: self-discipline and cunning must temper a warrior's rage.
  • Immerse yourself in whatever you hate, fear or shun, that it may not hold power over you.
  • Tempt, confuse and degrade others, that they may recognize their own limitations and seek to overcome them.
  • Maintain a veil of secrecy, for the Aeons delude humanity into fearing its own freedom.
  • Acquire power to further the cult's cause and turn the Aeons' dupes against them, but do not love power for its own sake.
  • Seek revelation through knowledge, faith and experience.

Virtues: Like followers of the Path of Typhon, adherents of the Path of Sutekh uphold Conviction and Self-Control.

Hierarchy of Sins (most to least severe):

  1. Refusing to aid in Set's resurrection — complete abandonment of sire, faith and clan to serve the Aeons.
  2. Failing to pursue arcane knowledge — the mysteries of enlightenment and the key to the Aeons' defeat may be hidden anywhere.
  3. Failing to undermine the current social order in favor of the Setites — the social order is a snare of the Aeons; only through Set can Kindred and kine find salvation.
  4. Failing to destroy a vampire in Golconda — those in Golconda are either ready to become independent creators or have completely sold out to the Aeons.
  5. Failing to do whatever is necessary to enlighten another — balking at any deed necessary to liberate another means you have not truly freed yourself.
  6. Failing to observe Setite religious ritual — this is akin to denying Set and faith itself.
  7. Failing to take advantage of another's weakness — how will others learn if they do not recognize their own demons?
  8. Obstructing another Setite's efforts — the ranks of the righteous are no place for petty power plays.
  9. Refusing to aid another follower of the Path — Set commanded his childer to cooperate against the Aeons; denying other seekers means denying Set.
  10. Pursuing one's own indulgence instead of another's — this shows a lack of self-discipline and compassion; enjoy your work, but remember you serve others first.

Excluded from this entry: the book's framing narrative (the fictional correspondence between the Setite historian Josué Pagnol/Manetho the Younger and his colleague, the account of the fictional cultist Marla/Renenet) is pure narrative flavor and is not reproduced here; only the doctrinal content it illustrates has been extracted.

pages.name: Setite Temple Organization: Founding Temples, Hierophants and Rank

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

The Followers of Set have no single worldwide hierarchy. Instead, the clan is organized as a loose federation of cults, each built around a Founding Temple and a number of lesser daughter temples. Most of the oldest and most prestigious Founding Temples remain in Egypt.

  • Hierophant: the senior priest who oversees a Founding Temple and, by extension, the cult built around it.
  • High Priest: the chief priest of an important daughter temple.
  • A priest who runs a small temple alone holds no title the rest of the clan is obliged to honor — any grander title she claims for herself is a private joke among Setites.

Eternal of Sirius (Djer Sopdet): Alone among the clans, the Followers of Set define an exact age of Methuselah-hood. A Setite who survives an entire Sothic cycle — 1,460 solar years, the period after which the Egyptian civil calendar realigned with the heliacal rising of Sirius (Sopdet/Sothis) — becomes a Djer Sopdet, an "Eternal of Sirius." Setites honor their Sothic Eternals as genuine demigods whose every whim carries the force of divine command. Mechanically, no Setite can hold clan Status higher than 3 without leading a cult and establishing a temple, and an Eternal of Sirius has an automatic Status of 5.

Setite Status factors: Setite Status derives from religious achievement as much as age. The most important factors include being a Setite in good standing with one's sire and local clanmates (base), leading a minor cult or chapter of a major cult, serving as an important cult officer in a major temple, leading a major cult and temple, elder status, knowledge of Thaumaturgy, renown as a Theophidian theologian (Setite Lore 4+), renown as an esoteric scholar (Occult or other esoteric Knowledge 4+), renown as a religious artist (Expression or Crafts 4+), and being a locally important favor-trader and power-broker (4+ in two useful Backgrounds).

Named Founding Temples referenced in this book:

  • Ombos — supposedly Set's own Founding Temple, destroyed by Sultan Baybars and secretly rebuilt in the 19th century; hidden from all but a few ancient Hierophants.
  • The House of the Eclipse (Cairo) — the "Eclipsan" doctrine holds that Setites must kill the sun-god Ra to become gods themselves; rumored to guard the clan's greatest trove of magic and lore.
  • The Red Temple of Thebes and the Garden of Asps (Memphis) — ancient but now nearly deserted temples, tended by a handful of elder priests guarding archives and artifacts.
  • The Crocodile Temple (Faiyum) — Founding Temple of the Cult of Sobek; keeps a pool of ghouled sacred crocodiles, one reputedly over a thousand years old and said to give oracles.
  • The Labyrinth of Bones (Tunis) — walls tiled with human bones looted from Carthaginian graves; rumored to hold staked Brujah Methuselahs excavated from Carthage.
  • The Descending Aerie (Tangier) — an enormous cavern carved so the wind hums a hymn to Set.
  • The Temple of Dogs (Isle of Dogs, London) — a joint venture of the Taweretan and Eclipsan cults, dominating Setite affairs in Britain.
  • The Cave of Apples (Naples) — official Founding Temple of the Cult of Typhon Trismegistus.
  • The Arena of Thunder (Abu Simbel) — Founding Temple of the Cohort of Wepwawet.
  • The Palace of Veil (El Kharga oasis) — Founding Temple of the Cult of Taweret.

pages.name: Setite Sub-Cults: Cohort of Wepwawet, Cult of Taweret, Sisterhood of Sekhmet, Cult of Typhon Trismegistus

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

The clan's flexible, experience-driven theology generates many distinct sub-cults. The most notable Western examples:

The Cohort of Wepwawet — A militant fundamentalist cult claiming leadership from Set's childe Wepwawet, based at the Arena of Thunder in Abu Simbel. Originally a cult of Warrior Setites devoted to defending Egypt, it grew rapidly in the 1960s on rumors that Wepwawet had woken from torpor, then launched a 1970s campaign to force heterodox Setite cults into line with "true and ancient" doctrine. The campaign backfired badly: it earned the Cohort the enmity of other major cults, drove the Afro-Caribbean Setites who became the Serpents of the Light into the arms of the Sabbat, and wrecked the Cohort's credibility. The shrunken Cohort now numbers many single-vampire cells and often targets rival supernatural "servants of the Aeons" such as Christian/Muslim sorcerer-priests and the Society of Leopold (with whom it fought a bitter vendetta in the 1990s). More than half of all Warrior Setites once belonged to the Cohort.

The Cult of Taweret — Based at the Palace of Veil beneath the El Kharga oasis, this cult claims Set's childe Taweret (goddess of fertility, childbirth and black magic) as patron and pursues liberation through the utmost extremities of sensation. Taweretans corrupt targets one at a time but choose victims whose ruin can cripple a company, topple a government, or otherwise cause public scandal; they never operate in groups larger than three, holding that the Aeons taint any bond not rooted in personal emotion. The Taweretans developed their own variant of the Path of Sutekh, which they call the Path of Ecstasy, favoring the Revelation of Ecstasy as the preferred route to communion with Set; Ecstatic Setites tend to cultivate Presence heavily and often dabble in Auspex. (Note: this Clanbook attributes the origin of the Path of Ecstasy to the Taweretans specifically; the mechanical Path itself is already documented elsewhere in this repository from Laws of Elysium.)

The Sisterhood of Sekhmet — Founded early in the 20th century by a coterie of female Setites as an all-female cult meant to recruit disaffected female Kindred (especially from the Camarilla, where princedoms were almost always male) toward Set. They chose Sekhmet, the lioness-goddess of war, plague and healing, as a symbol of female empowerment, framing the Revelations of the Void as ways of getting in touch with an inner "Lioness Power" and introducing Set only later as Sekhmet's consort. The cult only took off in the 1960s; of its roughly 100 members, only about a third are actually Setites (the rest come from other clans), and some initiates have splintered off to found cult cells with no Setite members at all. To the frustration of Setite members, no recruit has ever completed initiation all the way to the Path of Typhon/Sutekh.

The Cult of Typhon Trismegistus — The vehicle through which the Followers of Set first expanded into Europe, so influential that its Greek terminology ("Path of Typhon") became the clan's default vocabulary. Its origin myth syncretizes Set with the monstrous Greek Typhon, and further with Bacchus (ecstatic madness), Mars (war) and Pluto (the dead) — the three faces new recruits learn first, with the deeper truth that all three are masks of Typhon Set reserved for advanced initiates. Founded in Alexandria, the cult's Founding Temple moved to the Cave of Apples in Naples after the Purge of Baybars destroyed the original; it enjoyed a revival in the Renaissance and still dominates Setite affairs in Europe. In the last decade (relative to the book's late-1990s/2000 setting) several Typhonist shrines began sponsoring gladiatorial pit-fights for jaded Kindred and kine, secretly filmed for blackmail material — a practice that appalls more traditional, low-profile Setites even as it turns a healthy profit.

Excluded: anecdotal illustrative fiction about individual Setites (e.g., the Grand Copht/Cagliostro vignette, the Scandinavian Setite Arnulf Jormungandsson) is pure narrative color with no mechanical hook and is not reproduced here.

pages.name: Serpents of the Light: Organization and Ranks

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

The Serpents of the Light are the Setite antitribu of the Sabbat, an offshoot of the West African Cult of Damballah that took root in the Caribbean during the slave trade and eventually rejected Theophidian doctrine (including the divinity of Set) in favor of Sabbat sect politics and a syncretic Afro-Caribbean pantheon (Zarabanda, El Cristo Negro, La Madre de la Luna, Chango, Osanyin, Damballah and Aida-Wedo, Ogoun, and others, often equated with Catholic saints).

Organization and initiation: Following both the ancient Setite cult and many African faith traditions, the bloodline uses a system of many levels of initiation. Some grades are earned by mastering Serpentis, Obfuscate or Presence to a given level; others are purely social, granted for sufficiently generous gifts to the bloodline's elders. Each grade grants new "secrets" — recognition passwords, charms of no real supernatural power, and scraps of mythology — most of which are largely meaningless outside their symbolic and social function.

Named ranks:

  • Empereur — one of the four elders who hold the cult's highest initiation; the final three grades of initiation can only be granted with the unanimous consent of all four empereurs together.
  • President — the leader of a single Cobra cell.
  • Bête Serene ("Serene Beast") — a member of a cell in good standing.
  • Shampwel — the term for a single cell of the bloodline.

When a new cell forms, an empereur sends it a madoule d'estode, a miniature coffin emblazoned with a silver serpent encircling a golden star, to serve as the shrine's founding relic. A Cobra who reaches the fifth initiation learns the origin of the bloodline's name: it refers to the Milky Way, envisioned as a great shining serpent encircling the universe (not, as some assume, to any rivalry with the parent clan).

pages.name: Related Serpentine Lineages: Daitya, Tlacique, and West African Setites

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

Several vampire lineages share the Setites' Serpentis Discipline and susceptibility to light but developed into effectively separate traditions.

Daitya ("the Holy Blasphemers," India): Worshippers of Shiva the Destroyer who consider themselves a Brahmin caste of demons among the undead, tasked with a demonic caste duty to encourage every faith's adherents to violate their own religious taboos, hastening the Kali Yuga so that Brahma can create a new, purified world. Organization is by temple rather than sect politics; the most important social bond is to one's guru/Mentor (usually one's sire), and a Daitya remains subordinate until she demonstrably surpasses her guru in some supernatural achievement. Temples have complete autonomy, though older temples carry more prestige. The Daitya recognize only one lineage as a true "bloodline" distinct from the rest: the Nakrancharas, declared forever outcaste and defiled after converting to Buddhism and rejecting caste divisions. Clan Disciplines: Obfuscate, Presence, Serpentis. Weakness: shares the Setite sensitivity to sunlight and bright light. Daitya sorcery is called Sadhana (a practitioner is a Sadhu; its Paths are Siddhi, its rituals Tantras), learned through fasting, yoga and breathing exercises, and always sacrificed by fire.

Tlacique ("Servants of the Sun," Mesoamerica): A New World lineage descended from Tezcatlipoca that ruled Aztec, Incan and other Mesoamerican city-states openly as living gods, organizing native religion around mass human sacrifice which the Tlacique believed sustained the sun through its nightly death. Nearly destroyed by the Sabbat after an ill-fated alliance during the conquest era (Sabbat forces diablerized most of their elders, with Lasombra priests baptizing the staked victims first so they would meet Final Death in a state of grace); fewer than 200 survive today, scattered from Baja to Tierra del Fuego. With their pre-Columbian social order shattered, the Tlacique now default to Humanity rather than any distinct Path, and shifted real authority to their ancillae (who set policy), with neonates handling contemporary details and elders lending magical power and training. Status in the bloodline comes from mastering their form of Thaumaturgy (Nahuallotl; a Tlacique without it can never hold more than one dot of Status), from striking blows against the Sabbat, and from reviving traditional art or religion in mortal society — though true seniority still matters most. Clan Disciplines: Obfuscate, Presence, Protean (notably, not Serpentis). Weakness: as a hidden Setite-descended bloodline, Tlacique share the clan's sunlight vulnerability (an extra two health levels of sunlight damage, and a −1 die penalty from other bright light sources such as flares or spotlights).

West African Setites (Children of Damballah): Centered on a Founding Temple at Oyo (Nigeria/Benin, once capital of a Yoruba kingdom), this cult syncretized Set with Damballah-Wedo, a benign Yoruba creator-serpent paired with his wife, the rainbow-serpent Aida-Wedo. Centuries of isolation and torpid High Priests let Yoruba tradition wash away most Theophidian doctrine; only a handful of Damballan elders still remember the Egyptian connection, which is kept as a "Great Mystery" for senior initiates. Most Damballans now believe their powers and weaknesses come directly from Damballah-Wedo and Aida-Wedo rather than Set, treating Set as at most a junior third figure in their cosmology, and practice ecstatic trance-possession (drumming, dance, drugged blood) much like other West African diaspora religions. Attempts by the Cohort of Wepwawet to force the Damballans back into orthodoxy in the 1970s and 80s failed and permanently soured relations.

pages.name: Setite Worship: Temples, Ritual Categories, Holy Week, and Setite Lore

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

Temple layout: A typical Setite shrine has two chambers, representing Upper and Lower Egypt. In the outer chamber (Lower Egypt), celebrants symbolically shed their connection to the secular world — anything from washing their hands to stripping bare, confessing sins, and rolling in urine and ashes. The inner chamber (Upper Egypt, Set's demesne) is shielded from all exterior light, typically by a double set of doors or heavy curtains, and lit only dimly (guttering torches, colored glass, or hidden ceiling lights arranged as stars). Poorer Setites make do with a curtained-off room, a closet shrine, or a portable folding shrine carried in a black fabric-lined case.

Ritual categories (terminology from the Cult of Typhon Trismegistus, in general use among Western Setites): Bacchantic rites involve frenzied passion and abandon, seeking revelation through extremity of sensation; Martial ceremonies emphasize Set as warrior, exhorting the congregation to unite against the Aeons; Plutonian rites are solemn and meditative, reflecting on existence between life and death and godhood — most Embraces are performed as part of a Plutonian rite.

Setite Holy Week: The two most important festivals are the Murder of Osiris (the 107th day of the Egyptian year, corresponding to November 19) and Holy Week, the five intercalary days at the end of the Egyptian year (July 31–August 4), traditionally the birthdays of Osiris, Horus, Set, Isis and Nephthys, when the universe itself was believed to hang in peril. During Holy Week, Followers of Set pray for the doom of the gods and the end of the world, re-enact scenes from Set's life and unlife, report to each other how they weakened the Aeons' rule over the past year, and make new pledges. Many Setites deliberately keep chosen enemies alive until Holy Week so they can be sacrificed to Set on the Dark God's own birthday.

The Last Revelation (cult initiation structure): Setite cults almost never reveal their full doctrine to a new recruit at once. A recruit first receives a comfortable, watered-down doctrine; as she proves diligent, loyal and insightful, the priest reveals successive layers of "more advanced" doctrine, always explaining the previous teaching as merely incomplete rather than false. Only the highest grades of the priesthood ever learn the cult's full and, allegedly, true gospel — and even that may not be the final truth. This graduated-revelation structure is itself a deliberate psychological technique: by the time an initiate realizes she has been lied to at every stage, she has invested too much to easily walk away.

New Knowledge Ability: Setite Lore — Measures a character's knowledge of the clan's vast corpus of history, mythology, theology, sub-cults and rituals. Interpreting Setite religious texts, which are dense with mythological and philosophical allusion, may require a roll of Intelligence + Setite Lore. Non-Setite characters who somehow acquire even a single dot of this Ability are treated by the clan as a target for conversion or assassination if the Setites learn of it.

  • Student: You know that you assist the Dark God in opposing the Aeons, and can assist in your cult's liturgy.
  • College: You can discuss basic differences in cult theology and practice, and know much of Set's mythology.
  • Master: You can analyze Theophidian theology in detail, know the names of most Hierophants, and are privy to many secrets.
  • Doctorate: You know the specific goals of Hierophants and Eternals and have read many of the most secret texts and grimoires; the secrets of the Setites have scarred your soul.
  • Scholar: After such knowledge, what forgiveness?

Access to temple libraries: Large, old temples maintain libraries of esoteric lore, but access is not given freely even to fellow Setites — it counts as a Contact Background, obtainable directly or through a Mentor. A character must earn permission by completing a test or significant task set by the temple priests (e.g., stealing a grimoire from a Tremere chantry without detection, capturing or killing a priest's enemy, or delivering a sealed and possibly dangerous package without looking inside), followed by an initiation rite and an oath of secrecy. Setite temples do not lend out volumes or permit copying; many texts are written in Arabic, Coptic, or Egyptian hieroglyphic/demotic script and may require a priest's translation.

Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

Setite scripture (The Book of Going Forth by Night) describes the Nine Gates of Wisdom, called the Revelations of the Void, through which a devout Follower of Set attempts to strip away a victim's layers of self-deception and social conditioning (the "Chains of the Aeons") and lead them, deliberately, toward liberation and communion with Set. These are presented here as named doctrinal/narrative concepts for Storyteller and player use; none of them constitute new dice-mechanical Discipline powers (those are catalogued separately).

  • Revelation of Ecstasy — using extreme pleasure, pain, exhaustion or drugs (often in combination) to induce a trance that feels like direct contact with the divine.
  • Revelation of Terror — literally frightening the victim out of her wits so that, surviving, she feels reborn; often used as a classic initiation shock immediately followed by the image of the god.
  • Revelation of Wrath — goading the victim into towering, uncontrolled rage (a favorite of Warrior Setites), on the theory that blind fury strips away social conditioning as thoroughly as any pleasure.
  • Revelation of Desire — leading the victim to indulge and enjoy acts that revolt her, until she can no longer deny wanting them.
  • Revelation of Satiety — the opposite approach: over-stimulating a desire until it exhausts itself and curdles into disgust (though this does not work on chemical addiction, which merely breeds tolerance).
  • Revelation of Despair — discovering what the victim loves and values most, then destroying it or taking it away until all hope is gone, with the victim's pride and personal moral code as the ultimate targets.
  • Revelation of Ignorance — forcing the victim to accept something she previously considered impossible to believe about herself or her world (optionally including an inversion of her sense of good and evil).
  • Revelation of Chaos — destroying the victim's sense of living in an ordered, predictable world, typically via hallucinogens combined with real but senseless, tragic events, until Set's worship becomes the only fixed point left to build around.
  • Revelation of Blood — the Embrace itself: terror, ecstasy and desire together as the mortal dies, rises, and feeds for the first time; often reserved until after a mortal has already passed several of the other Gates and proven devotion.

A Setite who exploits a blood cult purely for personal gain, without providing any spiritual guidance in return, is contemptuously called an Osiris by more devout clanmates — a label other, less orthodox Kindred have since adopted generically for any parasitic cult leader.

pages.name: Setite Symbols of Faith and Recognition

text.content:
Source: Clanbook: Followers of Set

Because Setite blood cults must stay hidden from mortals and other vampires alike, they cannot advertise openly. Rather than the obvious cobra/snake iconography (which every Kindred already associates with the clan), careful Setites use more obscure references drawn from Set's mythology to mark property and recognize one another: Set's other totem animals (crocodile, hippopotamus, black pig), references to the constellation of the Big Dipper (which the Egyptians associated with Set), and allusions to storms, deserts, eclipses, beer, and lettuce (which the Egyptians considered an aphrodisiac tied to Set's virility). A Setite who wants to be found by other vampires might use blatant Egyptian or serpent motifs; one who wants to stay hidden avoids them entirely. Two strangers who each drop a few such references into conversation can use the exchange to feel out whether the other is a fellow initiate before speaking more openly.
